In the wake of his defeat to De Minaur, he said via Bild, “I started the tiebreak relatively poorly, made a few unforced errors, and then he didn’t play his way. That’s just how it goes sometimes.

“I thought the match was okay, but it’s been difficult for me to play here this year. The balls and the court are incredibly slow. De Minaur handles that better, and he was also better than me today.”

Ahead of the Paris Masters, tournament director Cedric Pioline issued some news that may not go down too well with the French Open and US Open champion.

The Frenchman revealed that the Masters 1000 competition will also use Dunlop balls this week, as the ATP Tour tries to implement a level of consistency over a sustained period.

He said at the weekend, “It’s a change imposed by the ATP, so that there is consistency across the entire autumn swing, from Shanghai to Turin.

“It’s good for the players’ comfort. I think it’s a good development, and the ATP has put in place a system whereby no event will be financially penalised by this imposed ball.”

Pioline has said that the court speeds will be quicker this year, after complaints were made about the slow conditions in 2025, when Zverev lost in the semi-finals.

Whether the speedier conditions will be enough to quieten Zverev’s dislike of the Dunlop balls remains to be seen. The 6ft 6in player begins his campaign with a tricky second-round match against the in-form Lorenzo Musetti, who owns a 3-2 head-to-head record in this matchup.

title: Boulter wins despite incident getting under her skin
article_text:
Katie Boulter said it was "lesson learned" as she overcame an incident that "got under my skin" to reach the last 16 of the Hong Kong Open.

The British number one was broken by Viktorija Golubic when serving for the match at 5-2 up in the second set.

During the game, Boulter complained to the umpire after a point was not replayed for an audible noise from outside causing a distraction.

An unsettled Boulter also lost her next service game before the world number 49 came through a tie-break to take a 6-2 7-6 (7-2) victory.

"It was interesting," said Boulter, who was the losing finalist at the Hong Kong Open in 2024.

"I was playing some really good tennis. I feel like I should have closed it out but a couple of things happened.

"There was a little bit of interesting judgement which got under my skin a little bit and, usually, I'm pretty good at batting it off but I was a little tired.

"It's end of season and it seemed to get to me but lesson learned, I managed to get over the line."

Boulter, who beat world number 89 Golubic in dominant fashion when reaching the semi-finals at the Japan Open last month, will play American Claire Liu in the next round.

Meanwhile, Venus Williams suffered a 17th consecutive singles defeat as she was beaten by fellow American Mary Stoiana in the first round in Hong Kong.

The 46-year-old, who is 597th in the women's rankings, lost 6-2 6-3 to 23-year-old Stoiana, who is ranked 113th.

Williams - a seven-time Grand Slam singles champion - has not won a singles match since July 2025 and relies on wildcards to play WTA tournaments.

Cameron Norrie progressed to the second round of the Paris Masters with victory over Italy's Matteo Arnaldi.

The British number two notched a 6-4 1-6 6-3 against Arnaldi, who is ranked nine places above him in 36th, in one hour and 41 minutes to secure his first ATP Tour win since August.

"I'm just trying to enjoy my tennis. It's been a difficult year for me and I don't really care any more - I just want to play, and play to win," Norrie told Sky Sports.

"I put a lot of expectation on myself to go and win, especially being a favourite [at times]. I was getting stuck a lot and I definitely want to try to change that.

"I really just want to play every point, enjoy every point, use my skills and give myself permission to let go and play to win. Be a bit more grateful to play."

Norrie, 31, was already a break up against Arnaldi when he lost his serve in the fourth game of the opening set.

However, the Briton immediately broke back before he served out to win it 6-4 in 36 minutes.

Arnaldi broke Norrie three times in the second set to level the match, but the Briton regrouped in the decider and, after securing a break to go 3-1 up, was able to hold his nerve to close out the match.

title: AJ Produkter pulls brand from IIHF World Championship over Russia’s entry
article_text:
The fallout from the revelation last week that Russia would be permitted to participate in International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) competition is already showing its face, as major IIHF sponsor AJ Produkter has broken its agreement with the body.

AJ Produkter, a Swedish workplace furniture and materials supplier, has sponsored the annual IIHF men’s World Championship for 37 consecutive editions, making it one of the body’s longest-tenured partners, but now says it will not be present at the event in 2027.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

The brand’s logos had appeared on referee jerseys throughout the competition, as well as rink-side dasherboards, and although AJ Produkter says that it will honor its contracted sponsorship obligations, it will not display its brand at the event.

Enock Johansson, AJ Produkter chair, explained: “Removing our logo after all these years is not a decision we make lightly. But our company has always stood for more than just commercial success. It is based on values, responsibility and doing what we believe is right. Sometimes that means making difficult decisions, even when they come at a price."

Last week, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled that Russia could compete in IIHF national team competition, and the federation acquiesced, albeit begrudgingly.

Despite the IIHF’s opposition to the ruling, Johansson continued: “Sport is based on rules. The referees make sure that the rules are followed on the ice. International law sets the rules between states. When a country so seriously disregards these rules, there must be consequences,"

AJ Produkter chief executive David Bray added: "Our decision is not directed against ice hockey, its players, referees or supporters. We respect the IIHF and are aware that the verdict was not the outcome that the federation wanted."

By comparison, earlier this month AJ Produkter maintained its sponsorship of the European Curling Championships, which barred Russia from participating.

The 2027 IIHF Men’s World Championship will be staged in Dusseldorf and Mannheim, Germany, from May 14 to 30.

Multiple national hockey federations have objected to the possibility of facing Russia, including Finland, which said it will outright refuse to compete against Russia so long as the war in Ukraine continues.

Finland is looking for support from other countries in the region who have already opposed Russian participation to support it and also refuse to face Russia.

The national federations of Austria, Czechia, and Germany have each already published statements decrying the decision and suggested they will mount opposition to the CAS ruling.

Perhaps ironically, it seems that Russia will take Ukraine’s place in the tournament, lining it up to face a number of disgruntled countries across Europe, including Finland, Sweden, Germany, and Latvia.

Other sponsors of the upcoming event include lubricants brand Liqui Moly, watch brand Tissot, workwear company Strauss, construction supply firm Wurth, and Patron Auto Parts.

It remains to be seen whether or not such brands will follow AJ Produkter’s lead.

AJ Produkter will still pay its sponsorship fee, but the removal of its brand poses a question for the IIHF about how far it may go before such decisions begin to affect sponsorship revenue and renewal rates from its long-term partners.

Russia has been banned from competing in many sports since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022. But the country appears to be slowly returning to the global sports scene, through both participation and hosting.

Last week, weightlifting became the first Olympic sport to bring global championships back to Russia after the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) awarded its 2030 Weightlifting Championships to Moscow.

title: Samson Adamu in as new CAF secretary general
article_text:
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) governing body has unveiled Samson Adamu, of Nigeria, as its new permanent general secretary.

Adamu has been acting in that capacity since March, following the resignation of the previous general secretary, Veron Mosengo-Omba.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

African soccer's governing body unveiled the news yesterday, with its president, Patrice Motsepe, saying that Adamu's permanent appointment came through a comprehensive recruitment process, and following the interviewing of several candidates.

Adamu has been at CAF since March of 2018, initially serving as director of competitions before then moving into the position of director of tournaments and events.

CAF has said he "brings considerable institutional knowledge and experience to this new role, in which he will oversee CAF's day-to-day administration and support the implementation of its strategic priorities."

Adamu's father, Amos, was a member of the FIFA executive committee for four years, before being banned in 2010 for breaking the global soccer body's anti-bribery rules.

Amos Adamu also spent time as president of the West Africa Football Union.

Late last week, it was unveiled that CAF had reneged on its decision to switch its high-profile Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) tournament to a quadrennial schedule. The tournament will instead stick to a biennial schedule – as has been in place since 1968.

CAF's executive committee “unanimously decided” to revert to the two-year cycle format, as the alternative, a ‘nations league’ competition, would take too long to make up the shortfall in revenue from the halving of AFCON commitment.

The last few weeks and months have also seen CAF looking to sell media rights to the next AFCON, scheduled to take place across Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, next June and July.

Late October saw a pair of agencies – Media Experts Limited (MEL) and Media Business Solutions (MBS) – snap up a package of exclusive free-to-air rights for the 2027 AFCON.

Through this latest deal, the agency pair will seek to identify FTA partners for the competition in all sub-Saharan markets, including in the three host nations.

Mosengo-Omba, meanwhile, resigned amid the fallout from the controversial 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) final.

He also avoided legal action in Switzerland in 2025 over alleged suspicious financial activities, after the Swiss Public Prosecutors' Office declined to open proceedings against him.

title: Murchie demands major improvement in Wales defence
article_text:
Defence coach Peter Murchie has called for a vast improvement in his area of the game when Wales resume their Nations Championship campaign on Saturday against Japan (16:40 GMT).

Murchie is preparing for his second campaign in charge of the defence after joining Steve Tandy's backroom staff from Japan side Kobelco Kobe Steelers.

In July, Wales defeated Fiji in Cardiff but lost to Argentina and South Africa, with the side missing more than 100 tackles and conceding 15 tries during the three games.

Murchie is expecting a lot more from the Welsh squad during the next month.

"From my side in the summer, we can be much better," said Murchie.

"I wasn't happy with the defence overall, there's much more in us and improvements to be made.

"We want to be extremely tough to break down and play against.

"The players are ambitious, they want to perform and defensively we want to be more consistent in our performances this November."

Murchie linked up with Wales after the conclusion of the Japanese Rugby League One season in June.

So having come into the backroom staff late for his first campaign, Murchie is hoping to make more of an impression.

"There is a much bigger lead-in than last time," said Murchie.

"We've got more of a complete coaching group and been able to debrief the summer properly and prepare.

"We have been out in the regions and it's been a good preparation to getting the boys into camp.

"We have had more time to build relationships and prepare this time around."

Murchie stated Wales must improve their win ratio having experienced only three victories in the 12-Test Tandy era so far.

Since November 2025, Wales have beaten Japan, Italy and Fiji and have lost the nine other internationals.

"We're here to win Test matches, we're not here to take part and we've spoken about that as a group," said Murchie.

"I'm not going to give you a number of wins.

"We're also looking for consistency in our performance in terms of delivery and performance in every game."

Wales will face familiar opponents on Saturday when they play Japan for a fourth time in 16 months.

Following the 1-1 series draw in Japan in July 2025, Wales won the game in Cardiff last November courtesy of a last-gasp Jarrod Evans penalty.

The hosts now have somebody in their coaching ranks who can give him some insight into a Japan national side coached by Eddie Jones.

"I've coached there last year, so know a bit about how they play and how they approach the game.

"During the last year or two, they've progressed and pushed numerous top teams close.

"We know the threats, the skills and pace, particularly the Japanese contingent, have which is what they pride themselves on.

"They've also got a big foreign contingent there who give them a different dimension, size and bulk, especially around the forward pack.

"It makes them a difficult proposition to play against and they've proven that in the Test matches they have performed against us.

"We respect them, they're well-coached and well-drilled, so we'll need to be at our best."

Murchie gave an insight into how Japan approach rugby.

"They are extremely hard workers with the way they're brought through high school nand university," said Murchie.

"They will train for three or four hours and it's no sweat off their back.

"They're used to extremely harsh training conditions and will run through brick walls for you.

"They are also very fit, skilful and throw the ball around."

After spending a year in Japan, Murchie outlined the differences of the Japan rugby culture.

"It's different to anywhere else in the world, the way they're taught and coached and it makes them makes a really interesting group of people to work with," said Murchie.

"I loved it, learned a lot and the rugby out there is completely different. You work for a company and I essentially I worked for a steel company.

"So you've got a real tie to them and you've got to learn as a coach to work with 38-year-olds, who have been there for 20 years, and Ardie Savea [New Zealand captain] in the same team."

title: McNamara to succeed Cullen as Leinster head coach
article_text:
Noel McNamara will replace Leo Cullen as Leinster's head coach from next season, the Irish province have announced.

Cullen said in June that he would leave his role at the end of the current campaign after a trophy-laden 12 years with Leinster.

McNamara is currently attack coach at Bordeaux Begles, who defeated Leinster in the Investec Champions Cup final last season.

The 43-year-old previously spent five years at Leinster in a number of roles, including Leinster 'A' head coach and as academy manager.

He joined the Sharks in South Africa in 2021 as attack and backs coach before taking on his current role with Bordeaux in 2023.

Since moving to France he has helped Bordeaux win consecutive Champions Cups and they have twice been runners-up in the Top 14.

In May, Leinster were second best as they struggled to deal with Bordeaux's McNamara-led attack in Bilbao, with the French side running out dominant 41-19 winners.

McNamara, who also coached Ireland to an Under-20s Six Nations Grand Slam in 2019, said that the job was "one of the most prestigious roles in world rugby".

"It is an honour to be given this responsibility," he said.

"We have a very exciting season ahead with UBB and I am fully focused on that before moving back to Leinster next summer."

Shane Nolan, Leinster's chief executive, said: "Noel has a long association with the club and emerged as our preferred candidate very early in the process.

"His transition into the role will be seamless and we look forward to welcoming him here next July after this season reaches its conclusion."

The IRFU's performance director David Humphreys said McNamara has a "deep understanding of Irish rugby".

"Noel brings a wealth of coaching experience, strong leadership qualities and a proven track record of developing players and coaching successful teams," Humphreys said.

"I'm looking forward to working with him to ensure Leinster's continued success, while supporting the development of players for the Ireland national team."

Since he took over in 2015, Cullen has led Leinster to six league titles and the Champions Cup in 2018, but his side subsequently lost five finals in the competition, including four in the past five years.

title: Northampton report record turnover in PREM-winning season
article_text:
Northampton Saints, historically one of the best financially managed clubs in the history of the PREM, have reported record turnover of £26.9m for the year ending 30 June, 2026. A decade ago in 2016, when the club enjoyed a 16th year of profitability, the club’s turnover was £16.61m, underlining how much the business has grown.

Buoyed by strong commercial growth and ticket sales, money gained from strong international representation and the spin-offs of hosting Women’s Rugby World Cup matches, turnover increased by £3.4m from the previous year, making it a successful year on and off the pitch for the PREM champions.

Saints’ financial report shows an underlying profit before tax of £0.2m. However, that result is affected by the accounting treatment of RFU academy funding, which has changed, and, as a result, the accounts show a reported loss of £0.9m.

A rise in the number of employees, all off-field, from 239 to 251, helped to inflate wage and salary costs by 5.8%, from £11.77m to £12.46m, Without this increase, Saints would have been very close to completely breaking even.

“Just as the team enjoyed a memorable year on the pitch, I am delighted to report that the Club delivered one of its strongest financial performances in recent memory,” said Ella Bevan, Northampton Saints Chairman.

“Underlying turnover reached a record £26.9 million during the year, an increase of £3.4 million on the previous season, despite the challenging economic environment in which all sports organisations continue to operate.

“A combination of sustained record levels of England EPS representation, additional home knockout fixtures, the successful staging of Women’s Rugby World Cup fixtures at DPD Stadium at Franklin’s Gardens, and continued growth across our commercial activities all contributed to this outstanding result. Ticketing, hospitality and retail performed particularly strongly, while our corporate events and non-rugby business continued to build momentum.

“I am equally pleased that this growth translated into improved profitability. On an underlying basis, the Club delivered a profit before tax of £0.2 million, representing an improvement of £0.9 million on the previous year. This progress reflects the hard work and commitment of our executive team, staff, players, supporters and commercial partners, and marks another important step towards long-term financial sustainability.

“Our balance sheet strengthened significantly during the year, with net debt reducing by £4.5 million and our cash balance increasing to £9.0 million. Combined with net assets of £23.4 million, this leaves the Club in a robust financial position and provides a strong platform from which to pursue our long-term ambitions.

“While we take great encouragement from these results, we remain focused on the work still to be done. Our priorities remain clear: to continue growing revenues, maintain financial discipline, invest in DPD Stadium at Franklin’s Gardens, and deliver exceptional experiences for our supporters, partners and visitors, while ensuring Northampton Saints remain competitive at the highest level.

“The progress made during 2025/26 provides further evidence that this strategy is working, and with a talented leadership team, a clear plan and strong foundations in place, I believe the Club can look to the future with genuine confidence.”

Saints’ financial report is another sign that the league is getting back on its feet after losing three clubs, Wasps, London Irish and Worcester in quick succession post-pandemic, and can hopefully now look forward to a more sustainable future.

As reported by RugbyPass last week, the league’s recently-revealed second annual Financial Monitoring Report says the league’s revenue in the 2025 financial year came in £7.8m above projections.

title: Home of Rugby League champions to host Test Rugby Union
article_text:
Whenever Wakefield and rugby union are mentioned in the same breadth, it’s normally as a reference to Wavell Wakefield, the former England Grand Slam-winning captain of the 1920s and RFU President, who was posthumously inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame in 2015.

Of a more recent vintage, RWC 2003 winner Mike Tindall was educated in the city, at Queen Elizabeth Grammar School (QEGS), treading the same corridors as England’s first RWC captain, winger Mike Harrison, whose moniker ‘Burglar Bill’ was born out of his capacity for scoring intercept tries and now lives on as the name of the monthly newsletter chronicling all things related to rugby union in Wakefield.

First-class rugby union in Wakefield pretty much died a death 22 years ago, on 22 April, 2004, when the Yorkshire city’s premier team was beaten 15-11 by Coventry at its College Grove home, resulting in relegation from National One and the club being wound up without barely any assets, other devoted super-fan, volunteer press officer and rugby historian, Richard Lowther.

While Rugby union does still have a presence in the Wakefield district, thanks to junior club Sandal, the loss of Wakefield RFC was a bitter blow to diehards like Lowther, who painstakingly puts together Burglar Bill, which is packed full of insights and anecdotes from a bygone age. Subscribers include former England boss Stuart Lancaster, who played in the black and gold of Wakefield before moving to Leeds.

One of the more curious links between rugby union and Wakefield that has attracted Lowther’s eye is happening this Saturday, not at College Grove but across the city at the DIY Kitchens Stadium, formerly known as Belle Vue before the commercial naming rights were sold. The match has prompted him to look at the history of international rugby in England’s largest county.

Lowther believes that Saturday’s Test match between Zimbabwe and Samoa, who’ve never met before, will be the first game of 15-a-side rugby to be played on the Belle Vue site – home to the current Super League champions, Wakefield Trinity – since Sandal played Sheffield there in 1948.

One thing is certain, it is the first rugby union test match to be played in Wakefield and the 12th in total in Yorkshire, dating back to the 1880s, when Cardigan Fields in Leeds hosted an England vs Wales match.

Exactly how Wakefield was chosen to be the venue, no one seems to know, but it gives rugby union a showcase opportunity in a city where rugby league is king, and ticket sales have been encouraging, with the Neil Fox MBE East Stand sold out in advance of match week.

After taking on Samoa, Zimbabwe’s next ‘home’ game will be in more familiar rugby union surroundings – Vallis Way, the home ground of leading Champ club, Ealing Trailfinders.

The Sables take on Uruguay at the west London venue on Saturday 14 November, before concluding their Nations Cup campaign a week later against Chile in Angoulême, France.

title: Key refereeing changes explained as rugby’s Nations Championship returns
article_text:

Top referees will clamp down on scrummaging technique in a bid to stabilise the set-piece during November’s Nations Championship fixtures as World Rugby seeks greater alignment in officiating across the sport.

Match officials in the 12-team competition, and the Nations Cup which sits beneath it, have been provided with specialist input from figures including former Wales captain Jon Humphreys and Warren Gatland to refine and clarify their processes.

Of particular focus will be on loosehead props ensuring they do not show a “tucked” right shoulder, with front rows encouraged to be temple-to-temple on engagement and ensure space is provided to tightheads to scrummage. The importance of the brake foot has also been emphasised in keeping players safe, while officials have also been asked to only reward teams who establish their dominance in a straight line, rather than at an angle.

There was significant discussion around the scrum during South Africa and New Zealand’s Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, with officials keen to preserve the contest as a key battleground.

All 24 head coaches were invited into World Rugby’s officiating camp to meet with decision-makers with a year to go until the World Cup, both with a view to ensuring clarity ahead of November and with a longer-term view towards the shape of the game.

The governing body’s data shows that ball in play time in matches featuring the world’s top 12 nations has swelled by more than two minutes since 2024, with stoppages down 10 per cent.

The average number of tries per game has increased from 6.3 to 8.2, with successful penalty kicks falling from 3.5 to 1.5 in a sign of an evolving sport. Changes in the kick-to-pass ratio also suggest that teams are more willing to play a greater number of phases with ball-in-hand.

Coaches are understood to have been relatively happy with the officiating of the breakdown, though World Rugby has moved to refine its head contact process to make decision-making clearer in that area. Mitigating factors such as a late change in dynamics will be considered provided a player arrives in control and attempting a legal clearout even if head contact is made.

Teams have also been provided with detail on the implementation of the “knee-drop” and “hip-drop” tackle laws. The latter of these will draw stiffer sanction should a player fall directly on the legs of a ball carrier having made a tackle from behind given the risk of serious injury. A challenge of this type made with significant force will be punished with a 20-minute red card.

A knee-drop tackle fails to stay on their feet before making a tackle, placing a knee on the floor. It will generally be sanctioned with just a penalty, and is unlikely to be strictly enforced around the try line as defensive players attempt to stay low and prevent the ball being grounded.

World Rugby is also separately planning to use biometric testing of fans to better ascertain supporter engagement within the sport. A research project is underway with hand-held sensors taking physiological readings to determine when watchers do and don’t engage, both in stadia and at home.

title: Paris Masters withdrawal list: 8 stars join Jannik Sinner by pulling out of the event
article_text:
This period of the ATP Tour season tends to be fraught with withdrawals, injuries, and illness, and the 2026 Paris Masters is no different.

The final Masters tournament on the ATP Tour calendar was rocked by the early withdrawals of the likes of Jannik Sinner and Joao Fonseca.

Felix Auger-Aliassime and Jakub Mensik confirmed they would not play the tournament before it began too, with the former ending his season early and the latter aiming to return for the Davis Cup.

After the tournament started there were several more withdrawals too. Flavio Cobolli confirmed he would not play the tournament, although he hopes to be back in time for the ATP Finals, if he qualifies for the event.

The second day of the tournament was rocked by two withdrawals, with both men set to play just hours later with the order of play already set.

Elsewhere, Alejandro Davidovich Fokina, who claimed the first Masters title of his career at the Shanghai Masters, continues to suffer with illness so he will not play the Paris Masters.

Davidovich Fokina had already been confirmed to miss the ATP Finals, so his latest withdrawal will not impact his upcoming schedule.

Tsitsipas has been replaced by Adolfo Daniel Vallejo, who will now play Learner Tien in his first round match at the Masters tournament.

Nuno Borges is set to step in as a lucky loser to replace Davidovich Fokina and he will play teenage wildcard Moise Koume in the first round.

Borges will not have long to prepare for his first round match at all as it is set to take place second on Centre Court on Tuesday, 3rd November’s order of play.

Playing against a home favourite in Kouame too, it could be very tough for the talented Portuguese star.

The Paris Masters is set to run from 2nd to the 8th November, with the likes of Carlos Alcaraz, Alexander Zverev, and Ben Shelton all in action at the ATP 1000 tournament.

title: Ben Shelton confirmed to join Carlos Alcaraz at ATP event in 2027
article_text:
The 2026 ATP Tour season is drawing to a close and eyes have already begun to turn towards the 2027.

Several top stars on the ATP Tour have already confirmed some of their early steps, including Alexander Zverev playing the Brisbane International and the United Cup announcing its lineup for the first tournament of the 2027 season.

Carlos Alcaraz, too, has been busy, confirming several events for his 2027 calendar, despite claiming he would play a limited schedule after the wrist injury he suffered in 2026.

The Spaniard is set to play the Rotterdam Open in February as he looks to win the ATP 500 tournament for a second time, after listing the trophy in 2025.

Alcaraz has also been confirmed to play Queen’s in June, after being forced out of the grass court tournament with injury in the 2026 season.

It has now been confirmed that he will be joined by Ben Shelton, who has also signed up for the ATP 500 tournament in London.

Shelton didn’t play Queen’s this year, instead opting for the Halle Open, where he reached the quarterfinals.

However, he does have precedent at the London tournament, although he does not have a good record at Queen’s.

In his three appearances at the grass court tournament, he has won just one match. That came against Lorenzo Sonego in 2023, before he was beaten by Lorenzo Musetti.

In 2024 and 2025, Shelton was beaten in the first round of the tournament, against Giovanni Mpetshi Perricard and Arthur Rinderknech.

Grass court tennis is by no means Shelton’s forte, as he has also struggled at Wimbledon throughout the years. He’s reached as far as the quarterfinals just once in his four appearances, which have also included a first round and second round exit.

The American did, however, win his first grass court title this season, at the Stuttgart Open. Shelton beat the likes of Taylor Fritz, Jiri Lehecka, and Marcos Giron to win the ATP 250 event, so he is clearly improving on the surface.

He will, of course, arrive at Queen’s next year with Juan Carlos Ferrero as his new coach, after making the announcement in early November that the Spanish coach would join his team in 2027.

As well as Shelton and Alcaraz, the ladies draw at Queen’s has also announced a new name for the WTA 500 tournament. Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova is set to appear at the tournament for the first time in her career.

The women’s draw was re-introduced at Queen’s in 2025 after 53 years and it has subsequently been won by Tatjana Maria and Donna Vekic.

title: Alex Mitchell out of Nations Championship opener in fresh England injury blow
article_text:
The Northampton scrum-half Alex Mitchell has been ruled out of England’s November opener against Australia on Sunday, with Bristol’s Harry Randall and Bath’s Ben Spencer called into the squad named by the head coach, Steve Borthwick.

Mitchell, established as the first-choice No 9 under Borthwick, damaged a hamstring in Northampton’s Prem win against Gloucester on Saturday and will have a scan on Tuesday to determine the extent of the injury.

Archie McParland, Mitchell’s uncapped clubmate, is also sidelined for the Wallabies match after sustaining a calf injury training with England last week, following his second call-up to the senior squad. A major scrum-half rethink is consequently needed by Borthwick before a highly significant sequence of four Nations Championship matches.

The injury-enforced absence of Mitchell and McParland means either Randall or Spencer will be on the bench against Australia, with Leicester’s Jack van Poortvliet expected to start at No 9.

While Mitchell is guaranteed to return when he recovers from injury, this week represents a priceless chance for Randall and Spencer to state their respective cases, with the World Cup less than a year away.

Borthwick and his staff will consider how swapping Mitchell and McParland for Randall and Spencer may affect tactics against the Wallabies. Randall is famed for a sniping running game with Bristol while Spencer, who recently returned to action for Bath after shoulder surgery, is known for his exemplary tactical kicking.

Elsewhere in the back division Gloucester’s Seb Atkinson, Exeter’s Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Fin Smith of Northampton are all named in England’s 36-man squad despite recent injury concerns. Max Ojomoh of Bath and Saracens’ Noah Caluori drop out of the group named eight days ago.

Meanwhile the in-form Harlequins fly-half, Marcus Smith, is widely expected to push his namesake Fin for the starting No 10 jersey while George Furbank, who is also in scintillating form for Harlequins, is a strong candidate to start at full-back.

There is one change to the forwards from the training squad named last week by Borthwick: the 21-year-old Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu, another uncapped player, drops out because of injury, with Theo Dan of Saracens returning.

Borthwick’s squad of 20 forwards and 16 backs gathered at Pennyhill Park on Monday night, with the Prem now on a break until December. After kicking off against Australia in round four of the Nations Championship, England will meet Japan and New Zealand in rounds five and six before the finals weekend at the end of November, with their last opponents to be confirmed.

“We’re looking forward to getting back to Allianz Stadium for four important Test matches against top-level opposition,” Borthwick said. “These fixtures take on added significance this autumn as they represent our final opportunity to face southern hemisphere opposition before next year’s World Cup.

“Facing Australia next Sunday is an exciting challenge. They have played a significant amount of Test rugby in recent months, and we know the quality and experience they will bring.”

Scotland have had a double injury blow of their own before the conclusion of their Nations Championship campaign, with Jamie Ritchie and Elliot Millar Mills ruled out of all four November matches.

Ritchie is expected to be out for four to six weeks after the flanker sustained a suspected medial collateral ligament injury in Glasgow’s United Rugby Championship win against Lions last Friday. The prop Millar Mills picked up a knee injury during Newcastle’s Prem defeat by Saracens on Saturday.

Three Edinburgh forwards – the props Ollie Blyth-Lafferty and D’Arcy Rae, and the flanker Freddy Douglas – have been called into Gregor Townsend’s squad. Scotland face New Zealand on Saturday before Tests against Australia and Japan, all at Murrayfield.

title: England hand surprise call-up to former Māori All Blacks forward
article_text:
England A have named their squad to face Argentina XV, with a former Māori All Blacks forward among the new additions.

Head coach Mark Mapletoft has selected a 30-man group for Friday's clash at The Rec, which kicks off at 19:45 and will be shown live on the England Rugby YouTube channel and Premier Sports.

The squad has been put together through a collaborative approach involving Mapletoft, senior England head coach Steve Borthwick and RFU Executive Director of Rugby Performance Conor O'Shea.

All 10 Gallagher PREM clubs are represented, with the England A squad assembling at the University of Bath training ground ahead of their first fixture of the season.

Newcastle Red Bulls forward Max Hicks is one of six players receiving their first call-up, having impressed since arriving in the North East this summer.

The New Zealand-born forward can operate at either lock or blindside flanker.

He started his professional career with Tasman before making his Highlanders debut in Super Rugby in 2022.

That same year, he earned a call-up to the Māori All Blacks, making two appearances for the side against Japan XV.

Hicks moved to France to join Perpignan ahead of the 2025/26 campaign but left in January 2026 to agree a two-year deal with Newcastle Red Bulls from the following season.

He is eligible to represent England through his ancestry, with his mother from Cornwall. He has not been capped at senior Test level by New Zealand.

The other new faces are Lucas Friday, Will Knight, Alex O'Driscoll, James Pater and Will Trenholm.

Bristol Bears' Fitz Harding will captain the side.

Eight players with previous senior England appearances have also been included: Charlie Atkinson, Jamie Blamire, Noah Caluori, Joe Carpenter, George Kloska, Luke Northmore, Max Ojomoh and Ethan Roots.

title: Youth Olympic Games: Czechia and Madagascar in medal hunt after a day of shocks in Dakar
article_text:
Australia, Kenya, Czechia and Madagascar will compete for the medals tomorrow with second seeds the USA sensationally out of contention.

The USA were beaten by Czechia and Madagascar in Pool B. The scale of the African nation’s 12-10 upset was seen in the players’ wild celebrations following their victory.

The results in Pool B also mean Spain are out of medal contention.

Pool A was also decided with one round of pool matches left to play as Australia and Kenya won their games against China and hosts Senegal.

The final pool matches - Australia face Kenya and Czechia take on Madagascar - on 3 November will determine the semi-final line-ups.

New Zealand, gold medallists in 2018, are not present to defend their title as they did not qualify for the competition. Therefore Australia are the favourites and top seeds, and recorded the most dominant result on the opening day with a 32-0 win over Senegal.

The competition began with a Pool A 12-5 match between Kenya and China with the latter's lack of discipline seeing the African nation capitalise. A yellow card was shown to Xinlei Guo after a series of penalties by China and being a player up Kenya scored through Evalyne Afande, which was the only score of the first half.

A beautiful solo effort from Michael Mmboga started the second seven minutes and another yellow card was given to China, this time for Yuyan Hu, with more repeated infringements. But Peng Songmei scored to give China a losing bonus-point.

Australia, who won gold in 2014, beat Senegal in the next match after tries from Te Rinajade Murray, Darci Mackay, Talia Berryman, Grace Buchanan and two from Mia Shelley.

Spain and Czechia got their tournaments underway with the first Pool B match seeing a tight second half make for an entertaining match. Czechia came out with the 35-17 win but both sides had standout scores; namely a wonderfully rapid try by Sofia Rodriguez and an amazing solo effort by Zuzana Svabova.

The final match of the first round of pool matches came between the USA and Madagascar. It was the closest game of the day with Sariaka Raveloarisoa scoring the winning try to see it end 12-10, the result somewhat of an upset.

After a break the pool games restarted with the hosts and Kenya locked in a scrappy and tense match as the score stood at 0-0 at half-time. Josephine Kerubo, Shaheen Sada and Afande scored to give Kenya the 19-0 win.

Australia also booked their spot in the final four with another victory, this time against China, despite a red card for Keira Callaghan. When down a player Australia struggled with three second half tries from China but Layne Prince made a huge play to seal the 21-15 win.

A close match saw Madagascar beat Spain 19-12, while Czechia overcame the USA 24-21 as the day’s action concluded.

The women’s competition will wrap up on 3 November with one more pool round followed by the placing matches and medal deciders.

title: PGA Tour finds new sponsor after Good Good fallout
article_text:
Two weeks ahead of putting on an inaugural tournament in Austin, the PGA Tour has a new sponsor for the event in the wake of the Good Good fallout.

On Monday, Compliance Solutions was announced as the presenting sponsor. Compliance is an accounting and tax service provider based in Longwood, Fla., and has an existing relationship with the tour, sponsoring Korn Ferry Tour and PGA Tour Champions events.

“We are proud to have their commitment and support as we prepare to bring this new event online,” said the tour’s executive vice president Dan Glod.

The move ends a whirlwind leadup for the tournament. In October 2025, the tour announced it was partnering with Good Good, a popular YouTube influencer brand and apparel company with a sizable following among younger golfers, to host a fall event. This would coincide with Golf Channel reviving the TV show “The Big Break,” which would confer a spot in the Austin field to the winner.

However in August Good Good released a promotional video that showed a man shoving a woman to the ground in a fight over a new Callaway driver. The ad, intended as a parody of the movie “Obsession,” drew immediate, far-reaching criticism, and was further inflamed by delayed apologies that many felt lacked accountability. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp called out the video during a press conference at the Tour Championship. “What we saw was concerning,” Rolapp said. “It is clearly not aligned with PGA Tour values.” He later added the company’s response was “a bit defensive and late.”

The PGA Tour ended Good Good’s sponsorship of the event while Golf Channel canceled its planned reboot of the “The Big Break.” Retailers including Dick’s Sporting Goods, Golf Galaxy and PGA Tour Superstore removed Good Good-Callaway merchandise from stores and their websites. After Callaway ended its partnership with Good Good, while Good Good’s top two executives were pushed out.

The Austin Championship begins next week at Omni Barton Creek Resort & Spa’s Fazio Canyons Course in Austin. It is the penultimate stop on the FedEx Cup Fall schedule, with the season wrapping up the week after in Sea Island.

title: Lee Westwood: I’d have been stupid not to join LIV – but I can see why it failed
article_text:
Lee Westwood has no regrets about taking LIV Golf’s money. But with his own future undecided, the former World No.1 believes the original operation wasted too much and still needs convincing about its proposed replacement.

Lee Westwood has defended his decision to join LIV Golf, saying the financial package would have been foolish to turn down, while blaming the way the business was run for the failure of its original model.

The former World No.1 has been with LIV since its first event at Centurion in June 2022. He still sees a future for the team circuit, but has signed nothing for next season.

At 53, he is weighing up rejoining the DP World Tour alongside senior golf, and how much time he wants to commit to either.

Speaking on The Chipping Forecast, Westwood discussed the money that persuaded him to leave, the loneliness of tour life and the shortcomings of the business he helped launch.

The podcast pairs broadcasters Andrew Cotter and Iain Carter with DP World Tour pro Eddie Pepperell, whose criticism of LIV has led to several public disagreements with his fellow Englishman.

This time, though, they had rather more room for debate than X’s character count. Here are the highlights of the hour-long conversation…

Westwood was among LIV’s original recruits, joining a field that included Phil Mickelson, Dustin Johnson, Sergio Garcia and Ian Poulter a stone’s throw from St Albans back in 2022.

He had turned 49 just a few weeks earlier. Whatever else the move represented, it offered a player approaching senior eligibility an extraordinary financial opportunity late in an already hugely successful career.

“A massive financial package was put in front of me – I would have been stupid,” he said of turning it down. “[But] that wasn’t solely the reason that I signed up with LIV.”

“I have no problem saying part of it was financial. I’ve made a fortune over the last four and a half years.”

The four-time European Tour Golfer of the Year says the money has left him in a position where he does not have to play again. Golf can now fit around his life, with considerably less pressure to keep earning from it.

Westwood was still competitive before joining LIV. He won his third European Tour season-long title at 47 in 2020, when victory in Abu Dhabi took him to 25 tour wins across four decades. In March 2021, he was runner-up to Bryson DeChambeau at Bay Hill and Justin Thomas at The Players, losing both by a single shot.

Westwood recalled how a subsequent break sent him sliding down the FedEx Cup standings. For a player living in Britain, keeping up meant either another lengthy stay in America or more transatlantic flights.

LIV offered fewer events and familiar faces, as well as the money. That combination suited him.

“I found it very lonely out on the European Tour and the PGA Tour,” he said, adding that he has “not a lot in common with a lot of the guys”.

He described taking people he knew away with him because the weeks and evenings otherwise felt so long. In one recollection, a younger playing partner recognized a song Westwood was humming as a remix rather than the original.

“I suddenly realized that they weren’t born in the 90s,” he said.

LIV’s original operation is now being wound down as the organization attempts to establish a new business under different ownership.

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund decided in April to end further equity funding, having bankrolled the league’s rise to the tune of billions. LIV subsequently entered a Chapter 11 restructuring process in the United States on September 8 and announced an agreement with BC Partners Credit for a proposed recapitalization.

Under the proposal, players would become majority owners of the reorganized business. LIV have said they intend to begin the next phase in early 2027, subject to court and stakeholder approval.

A host of players have already decided their futures lie elsewhere – Jon Rahm the biggest of those. Westwood’s Majesticks co-captain Ian Poulter is another, along with the likes of Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin, and Louis Oosthuizen. Westwood, meanwhile, is still waiting to be persuaded by what comes next.

“I think it was the running of it more than anything,” he told The Chipping Forecast when asked why LIV had failed.

“I think the way the business was structured, there was too much waste, really. I think there is a business there.”

He pointed to Australia and South Africa as examples of an appetite for the product, arguing that the more relaxed atmosphere, concerts and activities for children had helped attract families and younger spectators.

Westwood believes those tournaments showed a market for a different kind of golf event, and sees scope for a revised operation to make it work.

“I think if LIV 2.0 gets off the ground, it will be a successful business,” he said. “And I think they’ll still have great tournaments like that, which kind of takes me back to the very start of it. Surely with a 52-week year, there was room in the calendar for 14 events.

“But how much was the discussion had [to make it work with the other tours]? You know, it felt like when LIV came on the scene, the door was pretty much slammed shut straight away.”

Westwood said he got the feeling of “an us and them” and doesn’t believe there were any serious conversations between the various tours and the authorities in the game about how they could all operate cohesively.

title: Pro Kabaddi League's future uncertain as Season 13 pushed to 2027
article_text:
The Pro Kabaddi League faces a year-long break after its broadcast deal negotiations hit a roadblock. A reported 50% cut in the media rights offer has left Season 13 delayed until 2027.

The Pro Kabaddi League, once hailed as India's biggest sporting success story after the IPL, is facing an uncertain future, with its 13th season set to be pushed back by a year amid a stalemate over media rights. The league is expected to skip 2026 and return only in the June-July 2027 window, according to reports, after negotiations with current broadcaster JioStar failed to produce a fresh agreement.

According to reports, the sticking point is understood to be money. JioStar has reportedly offered just half of the previous five-year media rights deal, valued at approximately Rs 905 crore ($95 million). The previous agreement, which covered Seasons 8 to 12, ended with the conclusion of the 12th edition in October 2025. The league has since been without a broadcast partner, leaving its commercial future hanging in the balance.

Dabang Delhi clinched their second PKL title last October, beating Puneri Paltan 31-28 in the final at the Thyagaraj Indoor Stadium in New Delhi. But there has been little clarity on when the teams will return to action. Negotiations for a new media rights agreement have failed to make progress, Khel Now reported.

There has also been no announcement from the organisers on the player auction, which is usually held a few months before the start of a season. 'There has not been much interest in the open market, and the new deal offered by the current broadcaster is half of the previous deal. So all parties have decided that we need more time, and we will not see PKL before June 2027,” a source close to the development told Khel Now.

The impasse has also prompted PKL franchise owners to approach the Sports Ministry for guidance, much like their counterparts in the Indian Super League did earlier this year. In May, ISL clubs had written to the All India Football Federation and the Sports Ministry, seeking a club-led structure after their commercial arrangement came to an end. Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya met representatives of the clubs in June and asked them and the AIFF to form a task force and come up with a commercial plan. The ISL has since started its 2026-27 season under a club-led model.

Launched by Anand Mahindra and Charu Sharma in 2014, the PKL quickly established itself as one of India's most successful sporting properties. Star Sports has broadcast the league since its inaugural season, which attracted 435 million viewers, according to Star's figures. Only the IPL, which drew 552 million viewers in 2014, had a larger audience that year. Star India subsequently acquired a 74 per cent stake in Mashal Sports, becoming the majority owner of the league. The PKL has often been described as India's second-most-watched sporting league after the IPL. With the broadcast deal unsettled, scores of Kabaddi players and fans are left in limbo. Both the Indian Men's Kabaddi Team and the Indian Women's Kabaddi Team won gold medals at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, completing a golden double.

title: L1VE Secures Exclusive Worldwide Immersive Media Rights to the Saudi Pro League
Top English coach backs Welsh bid to join Prem in plea to fix problem
article_text:
Exeter Chiefs boss Rob Baxter has reiterated his desire to see Welsh teams join Gallagher Prem, insisting English sides need more games.

Last week, WalesOnline broke the news Welsh Rugby Union bosses have expressed a strong interest in moving two teams from the United Rugby Championship to the Prem in England. That comes as the English league plans to expand from 10 clubs to 12 in the near future, having seen a handful of sides go to the wall in recent years.

Wasps, Worcester and London Irish all folded in quick succession a few years ago - reducing the number of matches that English clubs are able to play.

And, while the RFU and Prem Rugby's official line is that they are currently focusing on English teams in any future expansion, Baxter once again offered his approval to bringing Welsh teams into the fold.

“There’s no point in me backtracking on what I’ve said in the past," he said. "We need more teams in the PREM, and it seems like a very simple idea. If it happens, great; if it doesn’t, it doesn’t.

“I know it’s very complex as to why it can’t happen around TV deals and long-standing other contracts. Contractual things are in place.

"But I think everybody, everybody in the sport, knows that we would need more regular games through the season.

“We play through the Six Nations anyway in the PREM Rugby Cup.

"I think probably if there were 12 or 14 teams in the PREM, I don’t think PREM teams would have a problem playing through the Six Nations and the Autumn period. We used to do it.

“Once you know it’s happening and you build a season around that, you get on with it.

"As far as I’m concerned, whatever happens to create more games and a better competition, it would be a positive thing, whether that’s the Welsh teams or another avenue. I would obviously welcome it.”

Welsh rugby bosses have already held talks with English counterparts over the potential to join the Prem, a move which has sparked a threat of legal action from the URC. You can read more about that here.

This isn't the first time Baxter has backed Welsh teams playing in an English league.

Ahead of the season, he told WalesOnline that he was in favour of such plans.

"I think an Anglo-Welsh league would be brilliant," he said back in September. "I've been a big advocate of it for years.

"I think we all know clubs are struggling with the amount of games. Welsh clubs seem to be talking about not really wanting to be in the URC, because it's a financial burden.

"It ticks a lot of boxes. Prem clubs want more games. I don't want to talk for Welsh clubs, but they don't seem to really want the travel and disruption that the URC can cause.

"So there's a bit of an ideal nature to it all."
