title: Ryder Cup legend admits he is unemployed after LIV Golf uncertainty
Springbok Women lose ground in World Rugby rankings after second Ireland loss
article_text:
The Springbok Women have dropped back to 10th in the World Rugby rankings following their 38-17 defeat to Ireland at Athlone Stadium.

South Africa were undone by a hat-trick from Béibhinn Parsons, a brace from Aoife Dalton and a try from Erin King, capping a difficult WXV Global Series campaign for the hosts.

Across September and October, the Springbok Women secured victories over Italy and Spain but suffered back-to-back defeats to Ireland before losing to Wales. Ireland, meanwhile, have retained fifth place in the rankings.

Following the latest defeat, Springbok Women assistant coach Franzel September offered an honest assessment of his team’s performance.

“That was disappointing of course, but that also gave us a reality check on what is needed to trade blows with the number five team in the world,” he said. “They were clinical when they entered our red zone and made every entry count.”

At the start of 2026, South Africa had set their sights on breaking into the World Rugby rankings’ top 10. They achieved that milestone despite a 40-27 defeat to Ireland, but have now slipped behind Scotland to reclaim 10th place.

There were no other changes in the women’s rankings. England, meanwhile, avoided the possibility of dropping as low as third by securing a thumping 55-12 victory over the USA Women’s Eagles at Sports Illustrated Stadium on Friday night.

The Red Roses maintained top spot, with Claudia Moloney-MacDonald marking her return to the starting XV with four tries in New Jersey. Meg Jones, Mia Venner, Bryony Field, Maddie Feaunati and Sadia Kabeya also crossed the tryline in the win.

The Black Ferns retained second place following their 36-7 victory over France, while Wales remained 11th after beating Japan 29-5 in Kumagaya on Saturday.

With the women’s international Test window now closed, there will be no further movement in the World Rugby women’s rankings until 2027.

title: Technicality could allow Christ Tshiunza play for Wales and Sale Sharks
article_text:
Sale Sharks boss Alex Sanderson admits he’s made getting his in-form flanker, Christ Tshiunza, on the plane to the World Cup in Australia next year a priority.

Tshiunza, 24, has been in superb form for the Sharks since his move from Exeter Chiefs, but in the summer was ruled ineligible to play for his country because he falls 10 caps short of the 25-cap minimum to play outside Wales.

He fell victim to a little-known loophole in the regulations, which rules him out of selection after it was deemed that he turned down reasonable offers from the Ospreys and Cardiff to pen a one-year deal with the Manchester-based outfit.

Sanderson said he has spoken to Tshiunza, who won his last of 15 caps in a 12-45 defeat to the Springboks in November 2024, about staying with the Sharks beyond the end of the season.

He says Steve Tandy can pick Tshiunza if none of the four Welsh regions can match an offer from the Sharks, which Rhys Carre and Jarrod Evans have previously profited from.

“I haven’t spoken to Steve Tandy, but we’re definitely in consultation on how we can get him back into the Wales squad and playing in the World Cup is probably top of our agenda for Chris because he’s doing some good stuff for us, isn’t he?

“He desires and wants to play in the World Cup. He wants to play for Wales. And that’s going to motivate him to whatever decision he makes moving forward, but we’ve made it quite clear and obvious: we’d love him to stay.

“The one thing that takes that out of Wales’ hands is what price range we go in at. If it’s a price range above what they’re able to match, then you can play for Wales and will get paid loads of money here.

“But it’s whether or not that price level is something we can fit into our salary cap. That’s what we’re working through right now,” Sanderson told RugbyPass.

title: Tiger Woods to design new golf course on Long Island
article_text:
Most news stories about Tiger Woods these days involve speculation as to his playing future. Will he peg it in the Hero World Challenge next month? What about the Masters? Or the Old Course at St. Andrews, which will host the Open Championship in July?

Meantime, here’s something we know Woods will be doing: redesigning a golf course on Long Island.

On Monday, Woods announced that he and his design firm, TGR Design, have been tapped to reimagine an 18-hole private course in Brookville, N.Y., in partnership with the Armchair Collective, a private golf club company seeking to build a national network of architecturally distinctive courses in sought-after destinations.

The latest from Woods is also the newest twist in the long, winding life of Tam O’Shanter Club, a North Shore property that opened in 1962, only to be remodeled by Robert Trent Jones Sr. in 1968. In 1999, it was redesigned again, this time by David Postlethwait.

In 2019, the club was sold to a development company that planned to build homes on the course. Those plans were abandoned, though, after arsenic was discovered in the topsoil. The club closed in 2021, and no golf has been played on the property since.

Last year, Brookville amended its zoning code to allow for-profit golf clubs to operate in the village, clearing a hurdle for a return to golf. The Armchair Collective acquired the 148-acre property in September for an undisclosed sum.

Now, its vision for the property is taking shape. Plans call for a clubhouse, member cottages, a golf performance center and a 20,000-square-foot putting green inspired by the Himalayas course at St. Andrews. Clearing has already begun, with course construction set to start next spring.

The club sits in a golf-rich area, roughly 13 miles from Bethpage Black, where Woods won the U.S. Open in 2002 — a feat he referenced in a statement Monday.

“I have great memories of competing on Long Island, especially at Bethpage,” Woods said. “This region has an extraordinary golf course architecture tradition, and we look forward to contributing to that legacy with a course that players can enjoy for generations.”

Woods’ own playing future remains less certain. The winner of 15 majors and a veteran of seven back surgeries, among other physical setbacks, Woods hasn’t competed in an official PGA Tour event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon, where he missed the cut. The last time the public saw him hit a competitive shot was at the TGL Finals in March. Three days later, he was arrested after rolling his Land Rover SUV on Jupiter Island and charged with driving under the influence with property damage. Whether Woods will compete next month in the Hero World Challenge, the tournament he hosts in the Bahamas, has not yet been determined.

With other activities in a holding pattern, Woods has stayed busy with TGR Design, the firm he founded in 2006 whose high-profile projects include The Hay at Pebble Beach, Bluejack National in Texas and Trout National in New Jersey.

The firm is currently working on Bluejack Ranch, also in Texas, in collaboration with Beau Welling, and has a championship links layout planned for Northern Ireland, which would be its first course in Europe.

A name for the Long Island project has not yet been announced.

title: ‘The ticket is the gateway’: How destination events, sprint races and greater accessibility are changing the modern F1 fan
article_text:
In 2025, fans in 160 countries bought tickets to a Formula One Grand Prix, a 42 per cent increase from six years ago, according to data from Viagogo.

Around 160 million people a month visit Viagogo’s ticketing platform, and Formula One is now the company’s third biggest sporting category globally, behind soccer and the National Basketball Association (NBA).

With the sport enjoying an unprecedented wave of global popularity, Viagogo senses an opportunity to stimulate and serve even greater demand for tickets – delivering benefits for all parties, including the Alpine Formula One team it partners with.

“If we can help introduce them to motorsport, introduce them to F1, and then introduce them to Alpine as a team to follow, that’s a great win for both of us,” Shaun Stewart, vice president of open distribution at Viagogo, tells SportsPro.

Viagogo has learned a lot about the modern Formula One fan, how they interact with the sport and the evolution of the race weekend. There have been major shifts with not only who is following the sport, but also why and where they attend races.

Formula One says 57 per cent of all newly acquired fans are under the age of 35, while women account for 75 per cent of all new fans and now represent 42 per cent of its global fanbase.

“We have the same gender split in regards to purchases with us, essentially the 60/40 split that the sport sees itself,” says Stewart. “What we’re seeing a lot in the new buyer demographics is they skew a lot younger than they traditionally have for us.”

There is also no more reliable trigger for a surge in ticket demand than a home driver on the grid.

“The transactions in Argentina have been through the roof for us once [Franco] Colapinto joined Alpine,” Stewart reveals. “[Racing Bulls driver Liam] Lawson changed how many people from New Zealand are buying F1 tickets, [former F1 driver Daniel] Ricciardo did the same for Australia.”

As a result, Viagogo tracks what nationalities might appear on future Formula One grids to predict markets which will spike in demand. For example, Bulgaria is one to look out for with Nikola Tsolov next in line on the Red Bull young driver conveyor belt.

Fans are also increasingly keen on attending Grands Prix outside their home country.

“77 per cent of [British ticket purchases] are for races outside of the UK this year,” he explains. “[In Brazil], 98 per cent of our transactions are for outside of Brazil … China is just slightly behind at 91 per cent, and then Australia.”

This changes the landscape for promoters. They must both compete amongst each other for international attendees and ensure that they retain the loyalty of their domestic audiences. Another development is that fans aren’t just buying tickets for races based on geographical proximity, with the Middle East increasingly popular as destination events.

“[Qatar] is up about 73 per cent in regard to how many countries are buying tickets,” adds Stewart. “If you look at anything from grandstand tickets for the Middle East races all the way up through to F1 Experiences and paddock passes, they’re more affordable, easier to get to, and we hear that drivers are more accessible.”

This trend contributes to the overall shift towards Formula One becoming more than just a race for visitors. For Stewart, “the ticket is the gateway”.

“These are destination trips now, they’re three to five days in length,” he explains. “It used to be the demand was solely concentrated on the Sunday ticket … now people are buying three-day passes, they’re going on five-day trips [and] these are destinations where these become family trips.”

Viagogo therefore holds partnerships with the likes of Booking.com and Expedia to offer flights and hotels, showing that ticketing platforms are becoming part of the wider travel ecosystem. These multi-day trips also highlight the economic case as to why hosts are comfortable paying the eye-watering fees associated with Formula One.

The introduction of sprint races has also contributed to fans deciding to commit to more than one day at the track. Whilst the sprint format is controversial with some purists that prefer the traditional weekend schedule, it has proved a success. Indeed, from next season, Formula One will have ten sprint events, up from six in 2026.

“With sprint races, you see a ten to 20 per cent jump in the Saturday demand once you add a sprint race to the calendar,” Stewart reveals. “You’d love to have a sprint at every race.”

Operationally, Viagogo is maximising the benefit from this demand shift through open distribution. This looks to replicate the model seen in the travel industry – where airlines sell tickets through their respective sites, but also through global distribution networks like Expedia or Kayak – to remove the wall between primary and secondary markets.

Stewart expands: “Someone sitting in Buenos Aires can jump on a website and see F1 tickets for every F1 race in the calendar, it’s become a menu. … Our 150-plus different websites are all localised – local language, local payment. Sometimes the primary experience is just designed around one language or one user base.”

The argument is that the main barrier to attending Formula One races isn’t cost or interest, but access. Selling tickets through several channels removes that barrier and brings in buyers the sport wouldn’t otherwise reach.

For rights holders, this means they retain control over pricing and keep the ticket revenue, while reducing the reliance on middlemen. Viagogo simply charges a booking fee and covers payment and processing costs. This turns a leakage of value into a new revenue stream.

title: Sports Direct and Nike launch “Athlete Intelligence” Christmas campaign
article_text:
Sports Direct and Nike have launched their first brand-exclusive Christmas campaign. It is built around “Athlete Intelligence”, a play on AI that casts Erling Haaland, Leah Williamson, Dina Asher-Smith, Henry Pollock and rapper Aitch as Christmas gift advisers.

Titled ‘Unwrap Potential’ and created by agency Chaos x Magic, the campaign has the group help shoppers spot a family member’s potential and find a present to match. In the 60-second film, they identify a girl’s footballing ability and recommend Haaland’s Nike Phantom 6 Low boots, while Aitch asks the athletes for help choosing presents for his sisters. A series of gift guides fronted by the talent accompanies the advert.

The cast draws heavily on British sport. Williamson has captained England since 2022 and led the Lionesses to European Championship titles in 2022 and 2025, becoming the first England captain to lift two major trophies. The Arsenal defender was made a CBE in the 2026 New Year Honours.

Asher-Smith is the fastest British woman in history over 200m, a former world 200m champion and a three-time Olympian, and won the European 100m title in 2024.

Pollock has become one of English rugby’s most marketable players since making his England debut in 2025. The Northampton Saints back-row forward toured with the British & Irish Lions, was named player of the match as Northampton won the Gallagher PREM final in June, and signed a new contract with the club in September.

Haaland, Manchester City and Norway’s leading striker, brings Premier League and international reach, while Manchester-born Aitch extends the campaign into music and culture.

The campaign launched on 3rd November across television, social media, digital and out-of-home advertising, and in more than 900 Sports Direct stores internationally. In the UK, it will be promoted in stores through ELEVATE, Frasers Group’s retail media network, which reaches more than 32m customers through digital screens, connected TV and outdoor advertising.

The tie-up forms part of Frasers Group’s Elevation Strategy to strengthen Sports Direct’s relationships with major brands. Christmas is the retailer’s biggest trading period of the year.

Michael Murray, Chief Executive Officer of Frasers Group, said, “Christmas is our biggest trading moment of the year, and our first-ever brand exclusive Christmas ad with Nike is a powerful example of the Elevation Strategy in action.”

César García, Vice President and General Manager at Nike, said, “Sport has the power to change how we see ourselves and what we believe is possible. Our partnership with Sports Direct is built on a shared ambition to bring more people to sport.”

title: Rob Baxter not prepared to backtrack on 'simple' fix to PREM problem
article_text:
Exeter Chiefs boss Rob Baxter says he would welcome Welsh regions into the Gallagher PREM with open arms after the WRU expressed interest in joining an Anglo-Welsh league.

The Professional Rugby Board, which runs the professional game in Wales, was told last week that the WRU plans to explore moving from the United Rugby Championship across the Severn Bridge to play teams from England.

Baxter says that 10 sides aren’t enough for the Gallagher PREM, which dropped three teams after Wasps, Worcester and London Irish all folded in quick succession three years ago.

The PREM hopes to expand to 12 teams for the 2029-30 season and has a “long-term ambition” to grow further, and bosses have claimed that their focus is on using their existing pyramid and bringing Champ teams into the fold.

But the Welsh plan gets a thumbs up from Baxter, who believes PREM clubs would even be willing to play league games through one of the two international windows during the season, as they always used to, if it meant playing more games.

“There’s no point in me backtracking on what I’ve said in the past. We need more teams in the PREM, and it seems like a very simple idea. If it happens, great; if it doesn’t, it doesn’t,” he said.

“I know it’s very complex as to why it can’t happen around TV deals and long-standing other contracts. Contractual things are in place. But I think everybody, everybody in the sport, knows that we would need more regular games through the season.

“We play through the Six Nations anyway in the PREM Rugby Cup. I think probably if there were 12 or 14 teams in the PREM, I don’t think PREM teams would have a problem playing through the Six Nations and the Autumn period. We used to do it.

“Once you know it’s happening and you build a season around that, you get on with it. As far as I’m concerned, whatever happens to create more games and a better competition, it would be a positive thing, whether that’s the Welsh teams or another avenue. I would obviously welcome it.”

title: ‘It’s unbelievable’: Rassie Erasmus hits back at Bok issue ‘people are starting to talk’ about
article_text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has downplayed concerns over the age of his squad, saying it is the drum “everyone loves to beat.”

Erasmus named a Springbok squad to face Italy in Turin on Saturday containing 12 players aged 30 or over, and believes the age of his squad is now what “people are starting to talk about” rather than the results the world No.1s continue to produce.

It has nevertheless emerged as one of the main talking points surrounding the Springboks’ attempt to secure a third straight World Cup title in a year’s time.

Speaking to the media this week, Erasmus seemed well-prepared to tackle such questions about the age of his players, and pointed out that it only takes a handful of changes to his team for the average age of the squad to fall.

Moreover, he stressed that as long as the older players in his squad continue to perform, he cannot omit them.

“Everyone loves to beat the drum that the team is getting older,” the double World Cup-winning boss said.

“It’s unbelievable. It’s heartwarming when South African people are talking about are the team getting too old? The team that played five weeks ago against New Zealand had an average age of 32, the team that plays this weekend has an average of 29. So it’s two or three changes in a team, and that’s why I so thoroughly enjoy the South African supporters.

“If you go with Krappies [Morne van den Berg] and Sacha [Feinberg-Mngomezulu], and you go with Ethan [Hooker] and Canan [Moodie] and Kurt-Lee [Arendse] and Sebastian [de Klerk] and you go with Damian [Willemse], that team is 28 or 27.

“If you go with Cameron [Hanekom], and just make a few changes there with Emmanuel [Tshituka] and Ruan [Nortje] and you go with Cobus Wiese, that team is 27.

“People are starting to talk not so much about our results and where we are, they’re talking about how long can this team do it. And that’s been the interesting thing. It’s been tough to make sure that we keep on winning but also blooding some young guys. But we’ve never put out a young team there.

“I don’t know if that’s frustrating people but that’s certainly us slowly evolving and knowing that players are getting older, but as long as they perform. I feel that’s what the older players have done. Jesse [Kriel] keeps on performing. Damian [de Allende] keeps on performing. So you can’t not pick them.”

title: Novak Djokovic issues angry complaint to umpire during Paris Masters win over Valentin Vacherot
article_text:
Novak Djokovic could not contain his anger during his Paris Masters opener with Valentin Vacherot due to disruption from the crowd.

After more than two hours of play, where both players split the first two sets 7-6 (5), 5-7, Djokovic brought up break points on Vacherot‘s serve early in the decider.

However, the 39-year-old’s flow was interrupted as he complained about lights coming on just before he returned the 27-year-old’s serve.

In one instance, Djokovic could be heard saying with a great deal of frustration, “The light! Every time before the serve.”

When it happened again, he angrily said to the chair umpire, “You tell them to switch off the light before the serve!”

Want more from Tennis365? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for tennis coverage you can trust.

Djokovic went on to break Vacherot’s serve and then hold his own to make it 3-0. But at the changeover, the umpire wanted to get to the bottom of the issue.

The 24-time major winner then explained, “Just before the serve, [on a] big point, they [the crowd] want to film it, and then they switch on the lights.

“It happened there (pointing behind the server on one side of the court) three times on big points, and here twice (opposite end of the court). This crowd, just behind. Of course, the crowd.”

Initially, the umpire thought Djokovic meant the light was coming from the venue itself, but he eventually understood that it was coming from spectators and took note of the veteran’s pleas.

title: DP World Tour, WWE Press On in Middle East Amid Conflict
DP World Tour veteran issues ‘loyalty’ reminder amid LIV Golf influx
article_text:
Get the latest news, reviews, analysis and opinion, plus unmissable deals and exclusive offers. Please check the box of every email you wish to receive.

This week is quite the contrasting one out on the DP World Tour.

While the first of two lucrative, season-ending playoffs gets underway in Abu Dhabi, things are much different for those battling it out back in Europe.

Away from the glitz and glamour of the playoffs, where each of the 70 in the field will take a share of the $9 million purse, players are competing for much more than money – their tour card.

The six-round slog that is the Final Stage of DP World Tour Q School is taking place at Infinitum Golf in Tarragona, where the top 15 and ties will come through to secure their spot for next season.

There are not many tougher challenges in golf, especially with the quality of field opting to tee it up this time around. As to be a expected, an influx of LIV golfers have signed up, as uncertainty continues to loom over the league’s future in 2027 and beyond.

Elsewhere, a number of the tour’s most recognisable faces will also be in action in a bid to regain their rights, no more so than Pablo Larrazabal. The Spanish veteran is no stranger to success out on the Wentworth-based circuit, but a tough 2026 campaign means he is now battling for his future.

He is now required to forge the Q School route for the first time in 20 years, having not lost his card since first gaining it two decades ago. Fortunately it comes at a venue that is not only on home soil, but at one where he collected the seventh of his nine DP World Tour wins at the ISPS Handa Championship Spain in 2022.

“Well, it is a golf course that I played only once,” he told bunkered.co.uk ahead of his Q School quest this week. “I played four rounds of golf and ended up winning the golf tournament!”

This time around, though, things are of course different. Larrazabal heads to Tarragona on the back of ending his season with a 17th missed cut at last month’s Genesis Championship, which ultimately cost him his card.

It was a brutal end to a brutal campaign for the nine-time winner. “It was tough to realise,” he said of the sinking feeling of losing his card. Now for the first time, the 43-year-old’s schedule is out of his hands.

“I was speaking to my wife. I was saying that I know I am going to be able to play tournaments, but now it is tough to build a schedule. It will be that on some point on a Monday, they could call you and tell you that you can play.

“You then have to make a decision, so that is a little bit of the concern I have, the fact I now can’t plan my tournaments in advance.” Of course, he can help his case this week, by banking one of the cards on offer.

“I need to go and play the same way!” Larrazabal said of his Q School chances with a nod to his win at the very same venue four years earlier.

In 19 full seasons on tour, the 43-year-old has become a part of the DP World Tour furniture with 493 starts and nine wins his to his name. In that time, Larrazabal has seen plenty of change, most notably due to the power placed in the hands of the PGA Tour.

“It was my dream to play the European Tour, I never looked at the PGA Tour as my dream,” explained the Spaniard. “The European Tour has changed a lot. So many players, superstars, stayed in Europe.

“Now there isn’t a superstar that isn’t going to play the PGA Tour. That says a lot.” A key component of this is the financial growth that has benefitted those Stateside.

“In the old days, on the European Tour you used to play for €2 million,” said Larrazabal. “In America they used to play for $7 million. Now instead of €2 million we play for €3 million and in America, instead of $7 million they play for $20 million.

“The increases in the world of golf have been massive, but we are the ones who didn’t jump.”

The DP World Tour has positioned itself underneath the PGA Tour, having awarded its 10 top performers (not already exempt) a place on the US circuit for the following season since 2023.

The emergence of LIV Golf and its now former riches also did little to help the European setup according to Larrazabal, who teed it up in the breakaway league’s very first event back in 2022.

So much so, the veteran believes the DP World Tour has found itself dwindling in the pecking order. “Now it is definitely the third tour after LIV and the PGA Tour,” said Larrazabal.

That may well be no more, though, amid LIV’s struggles to roll out its 2.0 plans without the support of the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia (PIF) gone.

In a change of policy, the DP World Tour has now informed players that they can no longer play across both circuits, delivering somewhat of an ultimatum to those who remain on the fence for 2.0.

Additionally those at Wentworth have been in advanced talks with LIV players – both members and non-members – in regard to playing opportunities next year, with tournament invites expected to be on the table for those who currently do not have status.

title: Korea Open: Shida Begins Afresh
article_text:
Chiharu Shida‘s new chapter continued to gather momentum at the YEOSU VICTOR Korea Open 2026 as she and new partner Ririna Hiramoto booked their place in the second round with a 21-18 21-11 win over Chen Su Yu/Chen Han.

The pair had only recently made their debut together at last month’s French Open and arrived in Yeosu still searching for rhythm after a hectic spell away from the international circuit.

“After France, we only had about a week before domestic competitions and there wasn’t much time to practice together,” Shida told BWF. “When we arrived here (in Yeosu), it almost felt like we were practicing together again for the first time. I felt that lack of practice showed a little at the beginning, but our combination gradually improved as the tournament went on.”

For Shida, a former world No.1 who returned to competition this season after taking a break from the tour, the partnership represents both a fresh challenge and a chance to pass on her experience to a younger generation.

Hiramoto admitted she was initially intimidated by the prospect of partnering one of Japan’s biggest names.

“At first I was a little nervous,” she said. “She’s older than me and was also a senior from my former school. I wasn’t sure whether I would be good enough.

“But Shida was really good at communicating with everyone. She would start conversations and create a relaxed atmosphere and gradually I became less nervous too. I think that positive environment has helped us on court.”

The 20-year-old has already identified plenty she hopes to learn from her new partner, particularly Shida’s renowned defensive game and court craft. For her part, Shida believes the contrast between the pair could become their greatest strength.

“I want to embrace the energy and freshness that my younger partner brings,” she said. “The age difference gives us a unique appeal and there are so many things we can learn from each other. As long as we can make the most of each other’s strengths, I believe we can develop into a really good pair.”

Shida is not the only Olympic medallist starting afresh in Yeosu. While the Japanese star won bronze at Paris 2024 alongside Nami Matsuyama, men’s doubles world champion Wang Chang claimed Olympic silver with Liang Wei Keng. This week, both find themselves testing new partnerships as attention begins to turn towards Los Angeles 2028.

World champion Chang partnered Xie Haonan while his regular partner and fellow world champion Liang Wei Keng teamed up with Hu Ke Yuan.

Wang/Xie, both from the Zhejiang Province, the tournament marked their first international appearance together. Wang revealed that the pair had already established a good understanding on court, while Xie took a more measured view, noting that there was still room to improve their chemistry.

Wang explained that the decision to split the established partnerships was aimed at bringing together different playing styles and ideas, allowing players to learn from one another and compensate for each other’s weaknesses. Xie agreed, saying the new pairing had ‘helped broaden his understanding of different tactical approaches and shot-making decisions in match situations.’

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games firmly on the horizon, Wang shared his long-term ambition remained unchanged.

“I think our goal is still to win titles. Our biggest goal was simply to give our best in every round,” Wang said.

title: How Lakshya Sen Plans To Capitalise On Hylo Open Momentum
article_text:
'I'm keeping the World Tour Finals in mind, I'm still in the race. I feel the next two tournaments are important as I look to finish the year strongly.'

- Lakshya Sen aims to carry momentum from his Hylo Open victory into upcoming tournaments, targeting a strong finish to the season.

- Sen is focused on qualifying for the BWF World Tour Finals, needing to finish inside the top 8 in the rankings.

- The shuttler has been managing recurring niggles and a demanding schedule, but currently has no major injury concerns.

- Sen prioritises winning titles over chasing the world No. 1 ranking in the highly competitive badminton circuit.

- Staying fit, healthy, and enjoying his game are key priorities for Sen amidst a packed international calendar.

Fresh from his title-winning run at the Hylo Open, ace Indian shuttler Lakshya Sen is looking to carry his momentum into the upcoming tournaments as he targets a strong finish to the season, with the BWF World Tour Finals firmly in his sights.

Sen said the victory had provided a timely confidence boost after a challenging few months marked by injury concerns and a demanding travel schedule.

"I'm happy with the way I played in Hylo. Winning a tournament after the Australian Open feels really good, and I want to carry this momentum forward," said Sen, who rose eight places to reach the 10th spot in the BWF World Tour Rankings.

The 2021 World Championships bronze medallist has to finish inside the top 8 to qualify for the season-ending BWF event.

"We have another two to three weeks of tournaments coming up, followed by a relatively lighter schedule. I'm keeping the World Tour Finals in mind, I'm still in the race. I feel the next two tournaments are important as I look to finish the year strongly," said Lakshya who is spending a few days at home before heading to Japan and Hong Kong.

The 25-year-old from Almora, who reached the final of the All England Championships earlier this season, admitted that recurring niggles had affected his consistency over the last few months.

However, he said there were no major injury concerns at present and that he was being more cautious about managing his workload.

"It was a good performance at the All England as well. However, over the next two to three months, I started experiencing a few niggles and injury issues that kept me from performing at my best, although nothing major kept me out of any big events.

"Playing the World Championships in India and the Asian Games was a great experience. Obviously, the performances didn't go as planned, but I was ready and out there fighting. As an athlete, you want to win every tournament, so I'm happy that things came together last week.

"I had a couple of good performances, here and there, but again, there are certain matches where I was not 100% fit but for the rankings, you still got to compete in those. So, yeah, that is the challenge for every athlete out there, who is playing almost 365 days."

On managing injuries and regaining match fitness, Sen said constant travelling had left him with limited opportunities to experiment with his game in training.

"I tried to work on certain aspects of my game during the tournaments I played, but managing injuries was a bit of a challenge over the last three to four months.

"I tried a few different things to manage the workload. In the two to three months leading up to the Asian Games, I was preparing well and focusing on playing as many matches as possible.

"Those matches helped me regain my match fitness. At certain events, like the World Championships, I felt I was lacking match practice. Since then, I've played quite a lot of matches. Even last week, I played five matches, which helped me perform well in the semifinals and final."

Sen also admitted to being a little rusty at the start of the Hylo Open after skipping the French Open due to shoulder pain sustained at the Denmark Open.

"Since I had skipped the French Open due to shoulder pain, I was a little rusty during the first few matches at Hylo. It can be difficult initially, but as the tournament progressed, I became more familiar with the court and the playing conditions.

"The opponents were also top-15 players, so you don't want to have a slow start against players like Popov or Christie. As the week went on, my touch and feel for the court improved, and I started getting more comfortable."

Lakshya said his priority remains to win titles more than chasing world No. 1.

"It's quite competitive out there. Players in the top 15, 20 or 30 can beat anyone on a given day. It's very tough, and the matches are challenging right from the first day.

"A lot of players have become world number one this year, but more than that, winning tournaments remains my priority," he said.

With a packed international calendar making consistency difficult, Sen said staying fit and enjoying his game would remain his priorities.

"I just want to target to just stay fit, stay healthy and keep competing in tournaments. I want to win the biggest competition, but at the same time, it's very tough every week.

"I just want to continue this momentum ahead, playing well and going deep into the tournaments and then enjoy my routines on and off the court and during the tournaments really be focused on the routines rather than thinking about the results."

Pro-Boxing in sponsorship headache
article_text:
Renowned local boxing promoter, Thuso ‘Scud’ Khubamang told Sport Monitor that boxing has the potential to excel at regional and international level, just like athletics. However, he said the sport continues to suffer from a lack of support hampering its progress. “Athletics is doing well because they have support from the government and the private sector. The absence of television coverage for professional boxing events is also a challenge,” Khubamang said. He noted professional boxing relies heavily on television, arguing that live broadcasts attract sponsors while television rights provide an avenue for remunerating boxers. “We are in a tight corner due to the absence of television from boxing.

It was the first time for us to postpone an event, and also the first time we faced sponsorship challenges,” he said. Khubamang added that local promoters were largely staging events to keep the sport alive rather than for commercial gain. “As local promoters, we are just hosting events for the sake of boxing, not for profit-making. “When things were tough, the Ministry of Sport and Arts (MOSA) came on board, which made a huge difference,” he said. However, Khubamang noted that the repeated postponements had also worked in the boxers' favour, giving them more time to train and prepare for their bouts. Despite the setbacks, he said the event eventually went according to plan. During the competition, Kutlwano ‘Chino’ Ogaketse, 28, was crowned the new IBO All Africa Junior Welterweight champion after overpowering South African Aphiwe Mboyiya.

'The title is now open for challenge, but it will depend on Ogaketse whether he accepts a challenge or not. He has grown as a boxer and is a hard worker,' Khubamang added. Novak Djokovic issues angry complaint to umpire during Paris Masters opener with Valentin Vacherot
article_text:
Novak Djokovic could not contain his anger during his Paris Masters opener with Valentin Vacherot due to disruption from the crowd.

After more than two hours of play, where both players split the first two sets 7-6 (5), 5-7, Djokovic brought up break points on Vacherot‘s serve early in the decider.

However, the 39-year-old’s flow was interrupted as he complained about lights coming on just before he returned the 27-year-old’s serve.

In one instance, Djokovic could be heard saying with a great deal of frustration, “The light! Every time before the serve.”

When it happened again, he angrily said to the chair umpire, “You tell them to switch off the light before the serve!”

Djokovic went on to break Vacherot’s serve and then hold his own to make it 3-0. But at the changeover, the umpire wanted to get to the bottom of the issue.

The 24-time major winner then explained, “Just before the serve, [on a] big point, they [the crowd] want to film it, and then they switch on the lights.

“It happened there (pointing behind the server on one side of the court) three times on big points, and here twice (opposite end of the court). This crowd, just behind. Of course, the crowd.”

Initially, the umpire thought Djokovic meant the light was coming from the venue itself, but he eventually understood that it was coming from spectators and took note of the veteran’s pleas.

title: Hylo Open titles offer fresh start for PV Sindhu, Lakshya Sen
article_text:
found the perfect response on the court, ending their title droughts with impressive victories at the Hylo Open Super 500 badminton tournament in Saarbrucken on Sunday. While Sindhu continued her encouraging resurgence with another title, Lakshya finally broke free from a prolonged slump, making it a memorable double for Indian badminton.

For Lakshya, the men's singles crown carried special weight. He arrived in Germany on the back of six consecutive first-round exits in international events, a run that had raised genuine questions about whether he could rediscover the consistency that once marked him out as one of the circuit's brightest prospects. His previous final appearance had come at the All England Championships in March.

Saarbrucken changed the narrative. The Indian produced some of his best badminton of the season, getting past France's Toma Junior Popov and then Indonesia's Jonatan Christie in the closing stages. His straight-game win over Christie in the final underlined his improvement and served as a timely reminder of his potential. "The last two matches I played were against top-quality opponents, and I managed to beat them convincingly.

So, happy with the way I played and happy to win a tournament," Lakshya said.

His mentor, former international and coach U Vimal Kumar, believes the title could prove pivotal. "For Lakshya, this title could prove to be a major turning point," Vimal told TOI, pointing out that the youngster has had a challenging season since May and has struggled to sustain his best form. In his view, a tournament victory at this level can do wonders for a player's confidence, and the wins over Popov and Christie should give Lakshya the belief and momentum he needs.

Sindhu, meanwhile, added another chapter to her encouraging revival. The former world champion claimed her first title since the Japan Open in July, converting her third final of the year into silverware. She had finished runner-up at the French Open only a week earlier and carried that momentum straight to Saarbrucken. Vimal credits her improved consistency largely to the strength and conditioning programme she has been following.

"At the highest level of racket sports, a well-planned physical preparation programme is absolutely essential, especially when players are competing week after week," he said, noting that four tournaments in a row would have placed considerable physical demands on her.

With the year-end finals scheduled for December, Vimal feels Sindhu should now prioritise recovery and prepare specifically for the season-ending event, provided she has qualified. While he appreciated her growing consistency, he identified reducing unforced errors at crucial moments as the key area for improvement.

title: Erling Haaland, Ilona Maher and Lewis Hamilton among winners of inaugural Meta x SportsPro Athlete Honours
article_text:
London, UK – Soccer star Erling Haaland, rugby sensation Ilona Maher and Formula One great Lewis Hamilton are among the inaugural winners of the Meta x SportsPro Athlete Honours, a new recognition platform which celebrates athletes who are leading the way on social media.

With a specific focus on effective use of Meta’s platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, Threads and WhatsApp, the Honours spotlight standout athlete storytelling and gold-standard creativity across ten award categories, including Content of the Year, Best Use of Threads, Sporting Moment of the Year, Purpose in Practice and Breakthrough Voice.

The winners and honourable mentions in each category were selected by a panel drawn from SportsPro’s editorial staff and Meta’s Sports Partnerships team, with athlete content judged on creativity and craft rather than audience size and engagement metrics.

Haaland, 26, claimed the Global Athlete Award after going viral during this summer’s Fifa World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico. The Norwegian striker has gained more than 36 million Instagram followers since the tournament, winning over fans with self-shot content that showcased his playful personality and engagement with online conversations.

Maher, the most-followed rugby player on social media, won Best Use of Instagram, where her grid showcases her body positivity, women’s sports advocacy and gift for storytelling, mixing behind-the-scenes glimpses of athlete life with her much-loved lip-syncing videos and self-deprecating skits.

Hamilton was recognised for Content of the Year after capturing the attention of the sporting world with the unveiling of his very own Ferrari F40 through a body of beautifully crafted film and digital work shot by his long-term photographer Sulay Kelly.

This year’s honourees include 11 men and nine women, representing 11 sports and nine countries across five continents. Six competed at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games with four claiming gold medals, including US figure skater Alysa Liu, whose alternative style and candid self-expression on social earned her the title of Breakthrough Voice for 2026.

The full list of honourees, plus athlete profiles and examples of some of the best-in-class social media content posted in 2026 by this year’s winners, can be found here.

“We’re delighted to be recognising the winners in our first Meta x SportsPro Athlete Honours list,” said Cris Bowyer, Athlete Partnerships at Meta. “It’s been a truly historic year of sport and beyond all the successes, the records broken and the headlines, one clear theme has emerged; athletes are taking control of their narrative more than ever. They are telling their own stories, in their own words, to their own audiences.

“That’s exactly what the Meta x SportsPro Athlete Honours is about; celebrating the best-in-class storytelling that athletes are bringing to Meta platforms, and sharing them with the wider sports industry.

“It’s truly a privilege to work with such global athletes on a daily basis. The reaction from the award winners has been incredible to see and we’re all excited to see the conversation and debate that our 2026 Honours list brings!”

James Dickens, SportsPro’s Director of Content, added: “When we launched the Meta x SportsPro Athlete Honours, our aim was to recognise the craft behind athlete storytelling rather than simply the size of an audience, and this year’s winners show just how far that craft has come.

“What stood out most to our judging panel was the breadth of creativity across every category and every sport. These athletes are setting the standard for what great storytelling looks like, and we hope their work encourages rights holders, brands and athlete representatives to think differently about the role athletes now play as creators in their own right.”

title: Rugby sevens: Madagascar beat USA and Spain at Dakar 2026 · SNA
article_text:
One kick was the difference. Madagascar and the United States scored two tries apiece at Stade Iba-Mar-Diop on Monday, but only Sariaka Raveloarisoa landed a conversion, and it gave the Makis Ladies a 12-10 win. Two and a half hours later, the under-18 side beat Spain 19-12.

That already settles the arithmetic. The Americans and Spaniards have lost twice and cannot match Madagascar's wins, and the top two in each pool go through to the semi-finals. Unbeaten Czechia stand between Madagascar and first place on Tuesday at 10:24 GMT.

The official match sheets give three scorers. Raveloarisoa made 16 of Madagascar's 31 points, with a try and a conversion against the USA and a try and two conversions against Spain. Soa Landy crossed in both games, and Tracy Ftiavananomenjanahary added the third try against Spain.

This was also the team's first outing on an Olympic stage, the site Foot Gasy noted. Malagasy Rugby president Marcel Rakotomalala had framed the campaign in late October as one step in a long-term plan for the women's game.

RFI's correspondent watched them train at the Stade Maki in Andohatapenaka the week before they flew, after a mid-October camp in Tunisia. Coach Dina Razafindratsara described a squad of twelve with uneven backgrounds: some raised in rugby schools, others only two years into the sport.

Physiotherapist Zo Andrianantenaina was frank about the gaps. There is no proper nutrition support, she told RFI, and some players eat only twice a day. "Our strong point is the mental side," she said, in remarks translated by SNA.

Kenya are in the same position in the other pool after beating China 12-5 and Senegal 19-0, and meet Australia at 10:02 GMT on Tuesday. So two of the four semi-finalists will be African. Senegal, also beaten 32-0 by Australia, face China at 09:40 before the fifth-to-eighth bracket.

title: Tennis, ATP – Rolex Paris Masters 2026: Djokovic comes back to beat Vacherot
article_text:
6-7 (5), 7-5, 6-1: the seven-time champion came from a set down against Valentin Vacherot, who was three break points from serving for the match. At 39, Novak Djokovic keeps his Turin hopes alive.

For anyone who still had doubts: yes, Novak Djokovic still has a lot to give. The Serbian came from a set down to beat Monaco’s Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5), 7-5, 6-1 in 2 hours 35 minutes in the first round of the Rolex Paris Masters on Tuesday. “A lot of intensity today,” Djokovic summed up in French on court after the match.

At 39, the 10th seed and seven-time champion becomes the oldest player to win a match in the tournament’s history, ahead of Jimmy Connors, who was also 39 in 1991. He extends his own record to 51 match wins in Paris. Djokovic also ended a four-match losing streak at Masters 1000 level, the longest of his career. It was his first win at this level since he reached the fourth round at Indian Wells in March.

“It’s the first time for me here. It’s impressive, honestly,” he said of the Plenitude Arena, where he was playing for the first time.

The win keeps his ATP Finals hopes alive. He moves to 2,940 points in the Race to Turin, and needs at least the semi-finals to stay in contention. Only the title would guarantee his place.

The first set went without a break. Serving at 5-6, Djokovic saved three set points, then led 5-3 in the tie-break before losing the last four points, two of them on his serve.

Vacherot broke at the start of the second set to lead 2-0. Djokovic broke back at 2-2, then saved three break points at 4-4 that would have allowed the Monegasque to serve for the match. At 6-5, he broke on his first set point to level.

“Honestly, it’s a victory for the crowd,” Djokovic said. “There was a moment in the second set, a break point for him, we had a 15- or 20-shot rally. I found a good shot at the end.”

The third set was one-way traffic. Djokovic raced to 3-0, had a break point for 4-0 and took it 6-1 as Vacherot’s unforced errors piled up.

Vacherot had beaten Djokovic 6-3, 6-4 in the Shanghai semi-finals in 2025, on his way to the title. He arrived in Paris on a five-match winning streak after winning the Basel title on Sunday, beating Jiri Lehecka 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the final.

Djokovic will face Australian qualifier Rinky Hijikata in the second round. Hijikata beat Luciano Darderi 6-2, 6-2 on Monday.

Lakshya Sen Reveals Injury Struggles Behind Form Slump After All England Heroics
article_text:
Lakshya Sen said that constant travel and fitness issues limited his ability to experiment in training, forcing him to focus on workload management during a challenging few months.

In March, Indian men’s singles shuttler Lakshya Sen enjoyed a brilliant run at the All England Championships, beating Shi Yu Qi, NG Ka Long Angus, Li Shi Feng and Victor Lai before going down to Lin Chun-Yi in the final.

Despite missing out on the title, Lakshya capped off a memorable week in Birmingham with a podium finish.

But that brilliant run was followed by a string of first-round exits at the Badminton Asia Championships, Malaysia Masters, Indonesia Open, Japan Open, China Masters and Denmark Open over the course of the year.

While Lakshya had team medals from the Thomas Cup and Asian Games to show for his efforts, the repeated early exits at other tournaments were tough to ignore.

Then came the Hylo Open, and Lakshya broke a year-long jinx of not winning a title, having won the Australian Open last November.

“It was a good run at the All England, where I reached the final and I was in really good shape. But two to three months later, I began experiencing a few niggles and injury issues that kept me off the court," Lakshya replied to a query from News18 Sports during a media interaction.

“Thankfully, nothing was serious enough to make me miss the major events. It was a great experience playing the World Championships here in India and then competing at the Asian Games," Lakshya added.

The star shuttler admitted that the performances hadn’t gone as planned but said that he continued to give his best and fight for every victory.

“I am happy that I managed to win a title last week, my first since the Australian Open. It feels good," Lakshya said.

Speaking about managing injuries and regaining match fitness, he added that frequent travel had left him with little time to experiment with his game during training.

“I have been travelling constantly, so there has not been enough time to experiment with new things in training. I tried to work on certain aspects of my game during the tournaments I played, but managing injuries was a bit of a challenge over the last three to four months," Lakshya told the media.

“I tried a few different things to manage the workload. In the two to three months leading up to the Asian Games, I was preparing well and focusing on playing as many matches as possible," Lakshya added.

Having withdrawn from the Korea Open, which began on Tuesday, the star Indian shuttler will next feature at the Kumamoto Masters, where he will face Chinese Taipei’s Chi Yu Jen in the opening round.

Lakshya Sen revealed that a series of niggles and injury issues kept him off the court two to three months after his strong All England run, creating challenges in managing his workload and match fitness.

title: Lakshya Sen targets strong season finish, keeps world tour finals qualification in sight after Hylo triumph
article_text:
Lakshya Sen is aiming to build on his Hylo Open Super 500 triumph as he prepares for the final stretch of the badminton season, with qualification for the BWF World Tour Finals among his immediate targets.

The Indian shuttler enjoyed a successful week in Germany, winning his second Hylo Open title and becoming the first Indian male player to achieve the feat. The victory has also helped him climb into the top 10 of the BWF World Tour Rankings.

For Lakshya, the title has come at the right time after a difficult few months affected by injuries and fitness concerns. After returning to winning ways, the 25-year-old wants to carry that confidence into the Japan Masters and Hong Kong Open.

“I’m happy with the way I played in Hylo,” Lakshya said during a virtual media interaction. “Winning a tournament after the Australian Open feels really good, and I want to carry this momentum forward.”

The World Tour Finals remain an important target for the Indian. He needs to finish inside the top eight of the rankings to secure a place in the season-ending tournament. With the next two events approaching, Lakshya believes they could play a major role in deciding his qualification.

“I feel the next two tournaments are important as I look to finish the year strongly. So I’m happy to be home for a few days before heading to Japan and Hong Kong,” he said.

Lakshya’s year had started on a positive note with a run to the All England final in March. However, recurring niggles and injury issues have affected his preparations and consistency.

Although he managed to compete at major events, including the World Championships in India and the Asian Games, the results were not what he had hoped for.

“It was a good performance at the All England as well. I reached the final and was in good shape. However, over the next two to three months, I started experiencing a few niggles and injury issues that kept me from performing at my best,” he said.

The Indian admitted that managing injuries while travelling constantly on the international circuit was difficult. He also felt that the lack of training time affected his ability to work on different aspects of his game.

“Playing the World Championships in India and the Asian Games was a great experience. Obviously, the performances didn’t go as planned, but I was ready and out there fighting,” Lakshya added.

Lakshya believes playing more matches in recent weeks has helped him improve his fitness and confidence on court. “Since then, I’ve played quite a lot of matches. Even last week, I played five matches, which helped me perform well in the semifinals and final.”

Lakshya also admitted that he was a little rusty at the beginning of the Hylo Open after withdrawing from the French Open because of shoulder pain sustained at the Denmark Open. However, he gradually became more comfortable with the conditions. “As the week went on, my touch and feel for the court improved, and I started getting more comfortable,” he explained.

With several tournaments still to come, Lakshya is well aware that managing his workload will be equally important. “My main target is to stay fit and healthy and continue competing in tournaments,” he said. “Of course, I want to win titles and compete for the biggest honours, but I also understand how challenging it is to perform consistently every week.”

title: Tennis, ATP – Rolex Paris Masters 2026: Tien holds off Vallejo
article_text:
Fifteenth seed Learner Tien beat Adolfo Daniel Vallejo 6-3, 5-7, 7-5, seven months after the Paraguayan lucky loser had beaten him in Madrid. The American, who needs to reach the third round to stay in the top 20, faces Luca Van Assche next.

Fifteenth seed Learner Tien of the United States held off Paraguayan lucky loser Adolfo Daniel Vallejo 6-3, 5-7, 7-5 in 2 hours 22 minutes in the first round of the Rolex Paris Masters on Tuesday. He will face Frenchman Luca Van Assche in the second round.

Vallejo, who lost in the final round of qualifying, took the place of Stefanos Tsitsipas, who withdrew with a right shoulder injury on Tuesday. The Paraguayan had beaten Tien 6-4, 6-3 in the second round in Madrid in April.

Tien needs to reach at least the third round this week to avoid dropping out of the top 20 for the first time since his top-20 debut in May, according to the ATP. The 20-year-old reached the second round in Paris last year.

The American won his first ATP title in Metz in 2025 and reached the semi-finals in Montreal this season.

Van Assche beat Mariano Navone 6-3, 7-5 on Monday for his first win in Paris.
